status_summary: Congress funded the detention and enforcement-staffing asks in two reconciliation laws: P.L. 119-21 (2025-07-04) provided 45 billion dollars for ICE detention capacity and about 29.85 billion for ICE operations, and P.L. 119-98 (2026-06-10) provided about 38.5 billion more for ICE, per CRS. ICE detention peaked at 70,766 on 2026-01-24 per one analyst's reading of ICE data, and TRAC counted 65,765 people held on 2026-07-11 (70.6 percent with no criminal conviction), below the Mandate's 100,000-bed figure; 183,181 people were in Alternatives to Detention on that date. FOX Local reported on 2026-02-14, citing an internal ICE memo, a plan to reach 92,600 beds through mega-centers, regional processing sites and acquired facilities, with the mega-centers to be operational by 2026-11-30; whether this was built was not verified. DHS said in January 2026 that ICE hired more than 12,000 officers and agents, with a workforce near 22,000, without a split between ERO officers and OPLA attorneys. In place of the shall-detain statute the Mandate seeks, the administration reads existing law to require detention without bond hearings for many people who entered without inspection (BIA decision of 2025-09-05); per CRS nine circuits rejected that reading and two accepted it, and the Supreme Court agreed on 2026-10-01 to review the question.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159 directs DHS to allocate or contract for detention facilities and to detain removable aliens pending proceedings to the extent permitted by law.
P.L. 119-21 enacted with 45 billion dollars for ICE detention capacity and about 29.85 billion dollars for ICE operations and procurement.

Board of Immigration Appeals decides Matter of Yajure Hurtado, holding immigration judges lack bond jurisdiction over many long-present people who entered without inspection, following a 2025-07-08 ICE interim guidance memo.
DHS reports ICE hired more than 12,000 officers and agents in under a year, taking the workforce from about 10,000 to about 22,000.

FOX Local reports an internal ICE memo dated 2026-02-13 that plans 92,600 detention beds (eight mega-centers of up to 10,000 each, 16 regional processing sites, and 10 acquired turnkey facilities), with the mega-centers to be fully operational by 2026-11-30; AP reporting cited there says ICE bought at least seven warehouses and six other proposed purchases fell through.
P.L. 119-98 provides about 38.5 billion dollars for ICE, including 31.075 billion for enforcement, removals, detention-related maintenance, 287(g) agreements and legal staffing.
TRAC data show 65,765 people in ICE detention (70.6 percent with no criminal conviction) and 183,181 in Alternatives to Detention; 43,138 people were booked into detention in June 2026.

The Supreme Court grants certiorari on whether people who entered without inspection and were later detained in the interior can be held without a bond hearing (case named for respondent Barbosa da Cunha, from the Second Circuit); argument date not reported.

title: Fund 100,000 detention beds and 20,000 ERO officers; mandate detention
uncertainties: No ICE detention count after 2026-07-11 was retrieved. The workforce figure comes from a DHS statement relayed by local TV and is not split into ERO officers, HSI agents or OPLA attorneys. The 92,600-bed plan is known only from FOX Local's account of an internal memo and AP reporting, and I did not verify construction or opening of any mega-center. Not verified: weekly detention-capacity reports, any formal limit on alternatives to detention, the Supreme Court docket number and caption, and the argument date. The peak figure of 70,766 (2026-01-24) is one analyst's reading of ICE data.
